The 5-minute TTL is too short for this agent; switch every breakpoint to the 1-hour TTL so entries survive between turns
Content upstream of the breakpoint is rewritten on each request (e.g. an edited earlier message); diff consecutive payloads
`max_tokens` is set too high, which forces a re-write of the cache
explanations: In a healthy loop, reads cover the prior prefix and grow each turn, while writes are about one turn's worth. Writing the whole conversation each time is the unhealthy pattern.
Turns that run back-to-back keep a 5-minute entry warm. The problem is a prefix mismatch, not expiry.

Correct. Writes equal to the full conversation mean the prefix no longer matches what was cached. Common causes are history edits, nondeterministic serialisation, or a per-turn change high in the prompt. Comparing payloads (or cache diagnostics, where available) locates it.
`max_tokens` is not part of the cached prefix.

questions.stem: A document-review tool fires 40 parallel requests at once, all sharing the same 30,000-token cached prefix, and then each asks a different question. Usage shows all 40 requests paid `cache_creation_input_tokens` for the prefix, and none read from cache. Subsequent waves sometimes behave the same way. What change BEST fixes this?
options: Send one request first, wait until its response starts streaming, then fire the other 39 so they read the entry it wrote
Increase the number of breakpoints to 4 so each parallel request finds a different entry
Use the 1-hour TTL so the entry exists longer
Add a random request ID to the top of each prompt so the cache can tell the parallel requests apart and store each one
explanations: Correct. A cache entry becomes readable only once the first response begins streaming. Parallel requests sent at the same moment cannot read what the others are still writing, so warm the cache with one request, then fan out.
More breakpoints cannot create a readable entry before the first write completes.
TTL governs how long an entry lives after it is written. The issue is that no entry existed yet when the 40 requests started.
A unique ID in the prompt changes the prefix bytes and prevents any sharing at all.

questions.stem: An e-commerce platform must route every incoming support email to one of 12 queues. Volume is about 2 million emails per day, a 300 ms p50 latency budget, and accuracy is judged by a labelled eval set. Which model tier should the team evaluate FIRST?
options: The most capable (Opus-class) tier, because routing errors are costly
The fastest, lowest-cost (Haiku-class) tier, measured against the labelled eval set
Whichever model has the largest context window
A mix in which every email goes to all three tiers and the results are majority-voted
explanations: Start from the requirements. High volume, a tight latency budget and a simple, checkable classification task are the profile of the smallest tier. Move up only if the eval shows it falls short.
Correct. Classification and routing at high volume and low latency is the use case the fastest, cheapest tier is built for. Confirm accuracy on the eval before choosing.
Emails are short. Context size is not the deciding factor here.
Calling three models per email triples cost and breaks the latency budget for a task one tier can likely handle.

questions.stem: A research product needs to read about 300 sources per question, extract findings, and write a synthesised report that needs deep judgment. The team wants high quality at a sustainable cost. Which architecture BEST fits, before any eval tuning?
options: A top-tier orchestrator for planning and synthesis, with per-source extraction delegated to cheaper, faster workers
Use the most capable tier for every call, including per-source extraction, so quality is maximised at every step of the pipeline
The cheapest tier for everything, retrying the synthesis until a reviewer approves it
A different model for each turn of a single conversation, chosen by a router per message
explanations: Correct. When there is a lot of independent work to hand off, matching the tier to each sub-task is effective: frontier judgment where it matters, cheap fast workers for the high-volume extraction. Validate it on evals.
This pays frontier prices for mechanical extraction that a cheaper tier probably handles well.
Synthesis needs the judgment of a stronger model, and retry loops on a weak synthesiser add cost and latency.
Switching models within one conversation breaks the prompt cache (caches are model-scoped) and can drop prior reasoning. Choose the model per route or conversation.

questions.stem: A fintech configured production with a model alias that the provider documents as a moving pointer to the newest snapshot. One morning, output formats subtly change and a downstream parser breaks, with no deploy on their side. How should model selection be configured going forward?
options: Keep the moving alias but add retries for parser failures
Pin a specific snapshot model ID in production config, and upgrade deliberately after running evals on the new snapshot
Resolve the model at startup by taking whichever model ID appears first in `GET /v1/models`, and cache it for the life of the process
Pin the SDK version, which also pins the model behaviour
explanations: Retries cannot fix a systematic format change. The same input keeps producing the new format.

Correct. Production should run a fixed snapshot, so behaviour changes only when you choose to change it, with an eval gate. Note that every current Claude model ID, including the dateless ones, is itself a pinned snapshot. The aliases that resolved to dated IDs belong to older models.
Picking dynamically at startup makes the model choice even less predictable.
The SDK version does not determine which model the API serves. The model string does.

questions.stem: A team switches the `model` string in the code below from an older generation to a recent one and starts getting 400 errors. Which TWO parts of the request are the likely cause on recent models? (Select TWO.)

code.src:
resp = client.messages.create(
    model=NEW_MODEL,
    max_tokens=4096,
    temperature=0.2, top_p=0.9,
    thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 6000},
    system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    messages=history,
)

options: `max_tokens=4096`
`temperature=0.2, top_p=0.9`
`system=SYSTEM_PROMPT` passed as a plain string rather than a list of blocks
`thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 6000}`
`messages=history`, where the history ends in a user turn after several assistant replies
explanations: `max_tokens` is still required and valid.
Correct. Recent models removed the sampling parameters, and sending them returns a 400. Delete them, and steer behaviour through the prompt and effort.
System prompts are unchanged.
Correct. Manual `budget_tokens` thinking was replaced by adaptive thinking. Use `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}` with `output_config.effort`.
A conversation ending in a user turn is the standard, valid shape.

questions.stem: Older extraction code forces JSON by ending `messages` with a prefilled assistant turn containing `{`. After moving to a recent model generation, every call returns a 400. What is the recommended replacement?
options: Put the `{` at the end of the user message instead
Keep the prefill, but add an `anthropic-beta` header to re-enable it
Use structured outputs (`output_config.format` with a JSON schema) so the response is guaranteed to match the schema
Keep asking for JSON in the prompt, then use a regex to pull the first `{...}` span out of the text and parse that
explanations: A stray brace in the user turn does not constrain the output, and it may confuse the model.
No beta header restores last-turn prefill on these models.

Correct. Recent models reject a prefilled final assistant turn. Structured outputs replace the most common use of prefill (forcing JSON) with schema-guaranteed output. Assistant messages elsewhere in the history, for example in few-shot examples, are still fine.
Regex extraction is fragile defensive parsing. Structured outputs remove the need for it.

questions.stem: A new model generation is released in the tier the team already uses. Product wants to switch immediately because of headline benchmark gains. Which THREE steps should happen before the switch reaches 100% of production traffic? (Select THREE.)
options: Run your own eval suite on representative traffic, comparing quality, cost per completed task and latency
Apply documented breaking changes (removed parameters, prefill, thinking config) behind a flag
Keep the old effort setting exactly as it was, so the comparison between the two models stays like-for-like
Re-check token counts and context budgets with `count_tokens`, because the tokenizer may differ between generations
Skip the evals, since a newer model in the same tier is strictly better on every workload and every metric
Switch all traffic at once, so the prompt caches warm up on the new model as quickly as possible
explanations: Correct. Public benchmarks do not predict results on your workload. Measure on your own evals before switching.
Correct. A model switch is a migration. Fix 400-causing changes before timing or evaluating the new model.
Effort defaults and calibration can differ between models, so carrying a setting over is not like-for-like. Re-sweep effort from the new model's defaults.
Correct. A different tokenizer changes costs and context headroom for the same text.
Newer is usually better on average, but behaviour, verbosity and cost per task can regress on specific workloads.
Cache warm-up is trivial next to the risk of an unvalidated switch. Roll out gradually.

questions.stem: To save money, a chat product uses a per-message router: easy messages go to a small tier, and hard ones to a large tier, within the same conversation. Costs went up, not down, and latency on hard turns worsened. What is the MOST likely cause, and the better design?
options: The router is too slow. Replace it with a regex.
Every model switch restarts the prompt cache (caches are model-scoped); pick the model per conversation and vary effort instead
Small-tier models cannot reuse the history the large tier already processed, so each one resends the whole history at a higher per-token price
The large tier gets rate-limited when used only intermittently, so the team should request a higher rate limit for it
explanations: Router latency is small next to repeatedly re-processing the full history uncached.

Correct. Switching models mid-conversation means the new model re-processes the whole history at uncached prices (and may drop the earlier model's thinking). Per-turn effort changes are the in-conversation lever, and some models support them without breaking the cache.
Every tier receives the full history you send. The cost comes from losing the cache, not from a price difference on history.
Rate limits would show up as 429s, not as higher cost per conversation.

questions.stem: A voice agent's users complain about dead air before the agent starts speaking. Responses are short (about 60 tokens). The agent uses a large-tier model with adaptive thinking at a high effort level, and the prompt is already cached. Which change is MOST likely to reduce the delay before the first word?
options: Enable fast mode on the current model, which raises generation speed so the first spoken word arrives sooner
Raise `max_tokens` so the model is not rushed
Switch to the Batches API to free up capacity
Evaluate a lower effort level and/or a faster tier, since up-front thinking and model speed dominate here
explanations: Fast mode mainly raises output tokens per second, which helps long outputs, not time to first token. For a 60-token reply, the wait is before the first token.
`max_tokens` is only a cap. Raising it does not speed anything up.
Batch processing is asynchronous and makes responses slower, not faster.

Correct. With short outputs and a cached prompt, the wait is mostly thinking before the reply and the model's own speed. Lower effort means less thinking, and smaller tiers usually have shorter time to first token. Confirm quality on an eval.

questions.stem: A contract-QA service runs on the most capable tier at its default effort and passes its eval with headroom. Leadership wants a 40% cost cut with minimal quality risk. What is the BEST order of experiments?
options: Switch straight to the smallest tier and add longer, more detailed prompt instructions to make up for any capability gap
Lower `max_tokens` by 40% to match the budget target
Sweep effort down on the current model first; only if quality holds, step down one tier and re-sweep from its default
Move all traffic to fast mode and negotiate a volume discount, since faster responses consume fewer resources
explanations: Jumping several tiers is the riskiest change, and prompt patches rarely make up a large capability gap.
A tight cap truncates answers. It changes quality without reliably lowering cost per solved task.
Correct. Effort keeps the same model and is easy to reverse. Model changes come after, one step at a time, each validated on the eval.
Fast mode costs more per token. It buys speed, not savings.

questions.stem: A team receives a deprecation notice for the pinned model snapshot its production service uses, with a published retirement date. What should the team expect, and what should it do?
options: After retirement, requests to that ID will fail, so schedule a migration with evals well before the date
Anthropic will silently route the pinned ID to the newest model in the same tier, so no action is needed at all
The snapshot keeps working indefinitely but at a higher price
Only the Batches API stops accepting the model; synchronous calls continue
explanations: Correct. Retired models are no longer served. Plan the migration, including breaking changes, evals and a staged rollout, ahead of the date.
Pinned snapshot IDs are not silently remapped to other models. That is the point of pinning.
Retired models are removed, not repriced.
Retirement applies to the model, not to a single endpoint.

questions.stem: A coding-agent team is choosing between two configurations: (A) the mid tier at high effort, and (B) the most capable tier at low effort. B has roughly twice the per-token price. Which approach gives the MOST reliable decision?
options: Choose A, since a lower per-token price always means a lower cost per completed task, whatever the effort level
Choose B, because a larger model always finishes in fewer turns and therefore always costs less per task overall
Average both models' public benchmark scores and divide by per-token price, giving a quality-per-dollar ranking to pick from
Measure both on the team's eval: pass rate and cost per completed task, since price lists don't predict the ranking
explanations: A stronger model at low effort can match or beat a cheaper model at high effort on cost per solved task. Price lists alone cannot tell you which will win.
Sometimes true, but not guaranteed. It depends on the workload.
Generic benchmarks do not reflect your tasks, tool loop or failure costs.
Correct. Only your own measurements of pass rate and cost per completed task can rank model x effort combinations. This is why each model-and-effort combination should be evaluated, not assumed.

questions.stem: A healthcare scheduling assistant uses a mid tier. A Haiku-class trial cut cost by 70%, but the eval showed it missed multi-constraint scheduling rules 12% of the time, compared with 2% on the mid tier. A missed rule causes a staff-handled rebooking costing about $8. The mid tier costs $0.010 more per conversation than the small tier. Which choice is BEST on total cost?
options: Small tier, because model spend drops by 70% and that saving compounds across every conversation the assistant handles
Mid tier, but only because the latency is better
Small tier, with a retry on every response
Mid tier: the extra 10 points of failures add about $0.80 per conversation in rebookings, versus $0.010 saved
explanations: This ignores downstream failure cost. Model spend is a small part of the total here.
The mid tier is not usually faster than the small tier. The reason to choose it is failure cost.
Blind retries pay twice and cannot detect missed rules without a checker, so the failure cost remains.
Correct. 0.10 x $8 = $0.80 of extra expected rebooking cost per conversation, against $0.010 of savings. Cost per completed task must include the cost of failures.
